name: Posture / frame / body language
lead: In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities, "posture", "frame" and "body language" describe how a person holds and moves their body. Practitioners use upright, open and expansive postures to look taller, broader-shouldered, more athletic and more self-assured, because the way the head, shoulders and spine are stacked changes the silhouette others see and the impression of confidence a person gives off.

Posture work in these communities usually targets visible alignment: pulling the head back from a forward position, setting the shoulders back and down, and standing or sitting tall. Posture and body language are also discussed as an attractiveness signal, alongside "power posing", the popular idea that holding expansive poses boosts feelings of power.[1][2]

Research on posture reports that confident postures can influence self-evaluation and mood. Reviews find a reliable effect of power poses on feelings of power, while the hormonal and behavioral claims of the original 2010 study have not replicated well.[1][2] Separate physiotherapy literature has studied corrective exercise for forward head posture and rounded shoulders, and reports measurable changes in craniovertebral angle.[4][5]

angle.text: Upright alignment changes how tall and broad a person appears and how confident they come across. Community members pair posture work with back and neck training so the position becomes the resting default.

paras: "Posture" refers to the position of the head, spine, shoulders and pelvis at rest and in motion. "Frame" is community shorthand for the overall impression of a body: shoulder width, carriage, stillness and presence. "Body language" covers gestures, stance and movement that others read as confidence, interest or indifference.

Looksmaxxing forum users describe posture as a "multiplier" for the face and body, arguing that identical features look different depending on head position and spinal alignment.[8][9] One widely read thread frames the skull as a lever whose orientation depends on posture, and attributes forward head position to overactive upper traps and weak lower trap and back muscles.[8]

Practitioners point to several visual effects: standing tall adds apparent height, drawing the shoulders back widens the upper body, and bringing the head back over the shoulders changes the look of the neck and jawline. Some forum members also report that correcting forward head posture changes how the face projects in profile, and some debate whether it makes a recessed face look more or less recessed.[10]

Physiotherapy research defines forward head posture, rounded shoulders and thoracic hyperkyphosis as common postural patterns and measures them with angles such as the craniovertebral angle.[3][4] These measures are the closest clinical counterpart to what looksmaxxing communities call posture fixing.

Carney, Cuddy and Yap (2010) reported that holding expansive poses raised testosterone and lowered cortisol in 42 participants. Ranehill et al. (2015) replicated only the felt-power effect, and in 2016 Carney said she no longer believed the effects were real.[1] A 2022 review of 128 studies by Korner et al. found reliable effects on thoughts and feelings, none on physiology and unclear effects on behavior; Cuddy and colleagues' 2018 meta-analysis reported evidential value for postural feedback.[1]

Brinol, Petty and Wagner (2009) found that people writing self-descriptions in a confident posture rated themselves more favorably than those in a doubtful posture, and Riskind and Gotay (1982) reported more stress in hunched postures.[2] Open posture was rated as more capable in counseling settings (Ridley and Asbury, 1988).[2] Peper et al. (2018) reported better math scores with erect posture.[2]

A meta-analysis of seven randomized trials with 627 participants found that corrective exercise changed the craniovertebral angle in people with forward head posture and reduced pain.[5] A 2024 meta-analysis of exercise for upper crossed syndrome examined forward head posture, rounded shoulders and hyperkyphosis together.[4] A review of the link between forward head posture and neck pain reported a significant difference in adults with neck pain but not in adolescents.[3]

Forum members discuss posture across several threads, from basic how-to questions to long guides, and often link it with tongue posture (mewing), neck training and back work.[6][7] Some users describe posture as overlooked relative to surgery or skincare; others are skeptical of social-media posture routines.[7]

Studies of posture and mood exist, and power-posing trials are summarized above.[1][2] Exercise trials have measured changes in forward head posture, rounded shoulders and kyphosis.[4][5] No studies were found testing "frame" as defined by looksmaxxing communities.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org posture is discussed as a foundational, low-cost way to improve appearance and is frequently tied to jaw and neck position.[6][8]

claims.claim: Forward head posture held for years changes how the face and skull look
claims.believers: Proponents argue the head acts as a lever and that decades of forward position shape the neck and facial profile.[8]
claims.experts: Physiotherapy reviews document forward head posture and exercise-driven changes in head angle, but studies of facial appearance have not been reported in these reviews.[3][5]

claims.claim: Posture is an overlooked multiplier for the face and frame
claims.believers: Forum authors say upright alignment makes the same features look better and adds apparent height and shoulder width.[9]
claims.experts: No published trial has measured attractiveness ratings of posture correction in this sense; posture-psychology studies report effects on self-evaluation.[2]

claims.claim: Fixing forward head posture can make a recessed face look more recessed
claims.believers: One thread argues that pulling the head back exposes underlying facial recession.[10]
claims.experts: No clinical study has examined this.

claims.claim: Power posing boosts confidence and testosterone
claims.believers: Popularized by a 2012 TED talk and picked up in self-improvement circles.[1]
claims.experts: Replications support a felt-power effect but not hormonal changes, and the original first author has said she no longer believes the physiological effects.[1]

card.summary: Open, upright body language to look and feel more confident; feelings effects hold up, hormone and behavior claims do not replicate well.

quick.overview:
Posture and body language practices aim to project confidence through upright, open and expansive stances.

Studies show small effects on how powerful people feel, but the hormonal and behavioral effects reported in 2010 have not replicated well.
quick.mechanism: The proposed mechanism is postural feedback: body position influencing mood and self-evaluation.
quick.risks: No direct risks reported. Ongoing disagreement exists about effect sizes.
